item.title: Celery Is Overkill for Most Teams: Huey vs Taskiq vs Procrastinate in 2026
item.description: A two-person team deploys a background worker and ends up babysitting four containers, a broker cluster, and a scheduler process nobody on the team fully understands. That is the Celery tax, and it is why so many Python projects now reach for something smaller. The genuinely underrated alternative tier has three members, and every one of them shipped code within the last week: Huey (6,044 stars), Taskiq (2,355 stars), and Procrastinate (1,417 stars). They occupy three different points on the simplicity-versus-async spectrum, and choosing wrong means either rewriting your worker layer in six months or paying for a broker you never needed.

item.title: Go Task Queue Libraries: Asynq vs Watermill vs Machinery vs gocraft/work
item.description: When building Go backend services, you inevitably need to handle background tasks — sending emails, generating reports, processing uploads, or running scheduled cleanup. Rather than blocking your HTTP handlers, you offload these to a task queue. Go’s concurrency model makes it an excellent language for building task processing systems, and the ecosystem offers several mature libraries purpose-built for this problem.

item.title: Self-Hosted Task Queue Web UI: Flower vs RQ Dashboard vs Arena
item.description: Background task processing is a cornerstone of modern application architecture. Whether you are sending emails, generating reports, processing image uploads, or running scheduled jobs, a task queue decouples expensive operations from your web request cycle. But once you have Celery, RQ, or Bull running in production, how do you monitor what is happening? This guide compares three popular self-hosted web UIs for task queue monitoring: Flower for Celery, RQ Dashboard for Python RQ, and Arena for Bull/BullMQ.
